title: Prior authorization consumes physician-practice staff time

history.reason: Two AMA survey reports read directly; evidence articulates the problem. Not validated as a startup opportunity.

description: Physician practices must complete insurer prior-authorization (PA) requests before prescribing or performing many services, a recurring administrative task that survey respondents say consumes substantial staff and physician time.
customer_segment: Physician practices and their administrative staff; the practice-size mix of respondents is unknown.
context: Reported by physicians in two AMA surveys (late 2016 and 2025). Whether the burden concentrates in small practices, and who holds budget authority, is not established.

evidence.text: In AMA's 2016 survey of 1,000 physicians, physicians and staff spent an average of 16.4 hours per week on PA and completed an average of 37 requests per physician per week.

In AMA's 2025 survey of 1,000 physicians, PA took an average of 13 hours of physician and staff time per week, about 40 requests per physician per week, and 40% of physicians employ staff dedicated exclusively to PA.
Fax and telephone were the most commonly reported methods for completing PA in the 2016 survey.
Repeat PA for already-stabilized chronic patients was reported as common (80% sometimes/often/always) in 2016.
The reported time burden appears persistent across roughly nine years, though the two surveys differ in sample and wording.
Some practices may pay for tooling or services that reduce PA staff time.

alternatives: Fax and telephone (most commonly reported method in 2016).
Dedicated in-house PA staff (reported by 40% of physicians in 2025).
Existing PA software, clearinghouse and outsourcing vendors: not yet investigated.

contradictory_evidence.text: Both sources are from the AMA, which advocates for PA reform; the figures are self-reported and come from one interested party, so independent corroboration is missing.
The 2025 figure (13 hours) is lower than the 2016 figure (16.4 hours) among differently constructed samples; the trend is not established.
Insurer pledges (June 2025) and regulatory changes may reduce the problem; the AMA reports physician skepticism (33% expect meaningful change), but outcomes are unknown.

uncertainty: Unknown: practice-size distribution, which tasks are automatable, buyer and budget, willingness to pay, competitor coverage, and whether payer-side reforms will shrink the burden.
open_questions: Is the burden concentrated in small independent practices (reachable, low-cost buyers) or in large groups?
What independent (non-AMA) evidence exists on staff time per PA request?
Which PA workflow steps remain manual despite existing software, and why?
How will CMS and insurer reforms change PA volume by 2027?
next_actions: Find independent sources (CAQH Index, CMS rulemaking, academic time-motion studies) on PA cost and time.
Survey existing PA automation vendors and their customer segments from public material.
